pl-l4d12c3-d1e112.summary: Reports others who hold that Christ's body is essentially broken and divided, and yet remains whole and incorruptible.
claims: Some hold that Christ's body is essentially broken.

pl-l4d12c3-d1e115.summary: Notes that they draw this from Berengar's confession before Pope Nicholas and many bishops: that the bread and wine on the altar are after consecration not only the sacrament but the true body and blood of Christ, and are sensibly, not only in the sacrament but in truth, handled and broken by priests' hands and ground by the teeth of the faithful.
claims: Berengar confessed that Christ's body is sensibly handled and broken.

pl-l4d12c3-d1e121.summary: Answers that since Christ's body is incorruptible, the breaking and division can soundly be said to occur not in the substance of the body but in the sacramental form of bread, a real breaking in the sacrament, the species, not in the substance. One should not wonder that accidents seem broken though they are without a subject, though some say they are grounded in the air.
claims: The breaking is real but occurs in the species.
Accidents without subject can be broken.

pl-l4d12c3-d1e124.summary: States that there is a real breaking and division in the bread, the form of bread, as Paul says 'the bread that we break', since the form of bread is broken into parts while Christ remains whole and entire in each.
claims: The form of bread is broken; Christ is whole in each part.

pl-l4d12c3-d1e131.summary: Quotes Augustine: when Christ is eaten, life is eaten; who would dare eat his Lord? Yet he invites us; he is not killed to be eaten but gives life to the dead; he refreshes and does not fail; he lives when eaten because he rose when slain; when we eat, we do not make parts of him, though in the sacrament it is done so.
claims: Christ is not divided by being eaten, though the sacrament is.

pl-l4d12c3-d1e140.summary: Adds Augustine: the faithful know how they eat Christ's flesh; each receives his part; he is eaten in parts and remains whole, in parts in the sacrament, whole in heaven, whole in your heart.
claims: Christ is eaten in parts sacramentally and remains whole.

pl-l4d12c3-d1e146.summary: Adds that these are called sacraments because in them one thing is seen and another understood: bread and cup are seen, as the eyes report, while faith, to be instructed, holds that the bread is Christ's body and the cup his blood.
claims: In sacraments one thing is seen and another understood.

pl-l4d12c3-d1e152.summary: Concludes that the breaking and parts that appear occur in the sacrament, the visible species. So Berengar's words must be distinguished: Christ's body is sensibly, not only in the sacrament but in truth, handled by priests' hands; but broken and ground by teeth truly, yet in the sacrament only. There is real grinding and division, but Christ is whole in each part.
claims: Christ's body is truly handled, but broken only in the sacrament.
Christ is whole in each part.

pl-l4d12c3-d1e158.summary: Quotes Jerome: each receives Christ the Lord, and he is whole in each portion, not lessened by the many, but gives himself whole to each.
claims: Christ is whole in each portion.

pl-l4d12c3-d1e167.summary: Quotes Hilary: where a part of the body is, there is the whole.
claims: Where part of the body is, the whole is.

pl-l4d12c3.summary: Reports others who hold that Christ's body is essentially broken and divided yet stays whole and incorruptible, appealing to Berengar's confession before Pope Nicholas that Christ's true body is sensibly handled, broken, and ground by the teeth. Lombard holds that, since Christ's body is incorruptible, the real breaking and division occur not in its substance but in the sacramental form of bread, the species, even though these accidents are without a subject; Christ remains whole in each part. Augustine, Jerome, and Hilary confirm: Christ is eaten in parts in the sacrament and remains whole in heaven and in the heart; whole in each portion. Berengar's words are to be distinguished: Christ's body is truly handled, but broken and ground truly only in the sacrament.
claims: Some hold that Christ's body is essentially broken yet remains whole.
The breaking is real but in the species, not in Christ's body.
Christ is whole in each part.
Berengar's confession is to be read as breaking in the sacrament only.
